summary: This unit teaches you to prepare and present sandwiches for villa and hotel guests: plan an order, keep high-risk fillings safe, choose breads and fillings (including Jamaican breads), make closed, open, club, finger, wrap, pinwheel and toasted sandwiches, work on a production line, cater for allergies and special diets, and cut, plate, label, pack and store sandwiches safely.

blocks.p: A sandwich looks simple, but it is one of the most common ways that guests get food poisoning. Sandwiches are not cooked after they are made, and they are made by hand, from bread, spreads and fillings that may already have been cooked, cooled and stored. A villa kitchen may be asked for a quick lunch, a picnic for a day trip, afternoon tea, or sixty sandwiches for a wedding brunch. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.
Done well, sandwiches are fresh, neat and the same every time. Done badly, they are soggy, uneven, squashed or unsafe. So this unit is about **planning, safety, neat work and speed**.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen, such as a production line of finger and closed sandwiches for an afternoon tea (with a gluten-free tray), and a selection of hot and speciality sandwiches. The assessor watches your hygiene, temperatures, neatness, speed and teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When an order comes in, find out these facts and write them down:

ul: **How many** sandwiches or guests, and **when** they are needed (and where: on the property, by the pool, or on a trip);
**The fillings and breads** the guest wants, and any special cuts (crusts off, fingers, triangles);
**Allergies and special diets**: gluten-free, egg, milk, nuts, fish, vegetarian, vegan;
**How they will be eaten**: served at once, on a buffet, or packed to travel.

blocks.p: Use standard recipes and work from the number of sandwiches. A common guide, which depends on the recipe, is below.

head: Item
Typical amount for one sandwich
Example: 60 sandwiches
rows: Sliced bread (2 slices)
2 slices. A sliced loaf gives about 20 usable slices (the two end crusts are left out)
120 slices, which is 6 loaves; order 7 to allow for waste
Butter or spread
About 10 g across both slices
Filling
About 50 g (more for wraps and club sandwiches)
Salad leaves
1 or 2 leaves
60 to 120 leaves
Garnish for the platter
A small amount
A bunch of parsley or cress

blocks.note: These figures change with the size of the loaf, the thickness of the slices and the filling. Weigh and measure for each recipe, and follow the standard recipe: it keeps the sandwiches the same size and the cost under control. Check the sum twice.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Work backwards from the time the sandwiches are needed. Sandwiches are best made **as close to serving time as the work allows**, but the fillings can be prepared earlier.

head: When
Job (for 60 sandwiches for 11:00 a.m.)
rows: The day before
Order bread and ingredients; cook chicken; cool, chill and label it. Boil eggs, cool and chill them. Check allergies.
Early morning (about 7:30)
Wash hands; mise en place. Make fillings (egg, tuna, chicken). Wash and dry salad. Keep everything in the fridge.
About 8:30
Make the special-diet sandwiches first (gluten-free, egg-free), with clean equipment; cover and label them.
About 9:00
Set up the production line and make the main order. Cut, cover and chill.
About 10:30
Arrange on platters; label with fillings and allergens; keep chilled.
Serve. Record the time food was put out.

blocks.p: **Cost per sandwich = total cost of the ingredients ÷ number of sandwiches.** If the ingredients for 60 sandwiches cost JMD 9,000, one sandwich costs 9,000 ÷ 60 = JMD 150. Weighing the fillings (for example, 50 g each) keeps the portions equal and the cost steady.

ul: Check the store and fridge, and order what is missing in good time. Bread, salad and cheese may need ordering a day ahead.
Use first in, first out; check use-by dates.
Keep bread in a clean, dry place, covered, away from strong smells and pests.
Check bread is fresh: no mould, soft and not stale or hard.

blocks.h: Why sandwiches are a high risk

ul: They are **not cooked after they are made**, so germs that get on them stay alive.
They are handled many times, by hand.
Fillings are often high-risk foods: cooked chicken, ham, egg, tuna, shrimp and anything with mayonnaise.
They may stand for hours on a buffet, or travel in a hot car or boat, in Jamaica's heat.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Hold a Food Handler's Permit; wear a clean uniform and hair cover
Required for every food handler in Jamaica; keeps hair and dirt out of the food.
Wash your hands before work and after raw food, bins, money, your face, hair or phone, and the toilet
Hands are the main way germs reach ready-to-eat food.
Use **tongs or clean disposable gloves**
Sandwiches are not cooked, so germs on your hands are not killed.
Change gloves when torn, or after raw food, bins, money or other tasks; wash hands before putting on a new pair
Dirty gloves spread germs just as dirty hands do.
Short, clean, unpolished nails; no rings, watches or bracelets
They hide dirt, and can fall into the food.
Waterproof blue plasters on cuts, with a glove
A blue plaster is easy to see if it falls in.
Tell your supervisor if you are ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or an infected sore, and stay off food work
You can pass the illness to guests.

head: Food
Temperature (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)
rows: Fillings, made-up sandwiches, mayonnaise, cut salad
Keep at **5 °C or below**.
Hot sandwiches (toasties, paninis) held for service
Keep at **63 °C or above**.
Cooked chicken and reheated fillings
Cook to about **74 °C**; reheat until piping hot.
Danger zone
**5 °C to 63 °C**: bacteria grow fastest. Keep food out of it as much as you can.

ul: Take out **small amounts** of cold fillings at a time and keep the rest in the fridge, so that the filling does not warm up while you work.
Never top up an old bowl of filling with new filling. Use a fresh, clean bowl.

**Cooked chicken** straight from the oven must be cooled quickly (spread on a tray, or in shallow containers), then chilled, before it is used in a filling. Warm chicken warms the mayonnaise and the other fillings.
**Hard-boiled eggs:** boil for about 10 minutes, cool quickly in cold water, peel, and chill.
**Cooked ackee and saltfish** used as a cold filling must also be cooled quickly and kept chilled.
**Mayonnaise-based fillings** (tuna, egg, chicken) are high-risk: keep them at 5 °C or below. Use pasteurised egg in home-made mayonnaise, or a ready-made one.
Wash salad leaves, tomatoes and cucumber, and dry them; wet leaves make the bread soggy.
Cover them with cling film or a lid, or wrap them, so they do not dry out or pick up dirt.
Label each tray or pack with the name of the sandwich, the date and time made, the use-by time and any allergens.
Store in the fridge at 5 °C or below, away from raw food.
For display, use a chilled unit or keep trays over ice. Put out a few platters at a time.
Record the time food goes out. Food that has been out longer than the plan allows (commonly 2 to 4 hours in total) is **thrown away**, and the amount is recorded.

blocks.note: Never put sandwiches that have been out on a buffet back in the fridge to serve again the next day. Once the time allowed has passed, they go in the bin.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Make the sandwiches cold, wrap them, and pack them in an insulated cool box with ice packs, at 5 °C or below, as close to leaving time as possible.
Keep the cool box shut and out of the sun and the hot boot of a car or the deck of a boat.
Tell the guests to eat within the time the Centre's plan gives (often 2 to 4 hours), and not to bring leftovers home to eat.
For long trips, choose sandwiches with lower-risk fillings, such as cheese and cucumber, instead of egg or tuna with mayonnaise, or wraps that are firm and travel well.

blocks.note: In the heat of Jamaica, a sandwich in a car or on a beach can go into the danger zone within a very short time. Pack ice packs, not just ice in a bag, so the water does not soak the sandwiches. Take food out of the box only when the guests are ready to eat.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Bread
What it is
Good for
rows: Sliced white or brown sandwich bread
A soft loaf cut in even slices.
Closed, finger, club (toasted) and open sandwiches.
Hard dough bread
A dense, slightly sweet Jamaican white loaf with a firm crumb.
Sandwiches of ham, cheese, egg or ackee and saltfish; toasted sandwiches.
Coco bread
A soft, slightly sweet folded bread.
A beef patty in coco bread is a well-known Jamaican snack.
Spiced bun
A dark, fruited and spiced loaf or bun.
Eaten with cheese at Easter ('bun and cheese').
Panini rolls, baguette, sub rolls, ciabatta
Crusty rolls.
Toasted sandwiches; hearty cold sandwiches.
Soft flour tortillas, wraps, pita (pocket bread)
Flat breads.
Wraps and pinwheels; pita is opened up into a pocket.
Bammy
A flat bread made from cassava, with no wheat.
A base for canapés and open sandwiches.
Gluten-free bread
Bread made without wheat.
Guests who cannot eat gluten.

ul: Bread should be fresh and soft, not stale, hard and dry. **Stale** bread has gone hard and dry from being left uncovered.
Slightly day-old sandwich bread is easier to slice thin and cut cleanly than very fresh, soft bread.
Check for mould (green or white spots) and throw away the whole loaf if you see any.

blocks.p: A spread, such as **butter, margarine or mayonnaise**, is put **thinly and evenly on the bread, right to the edges**. It does three jobs: it forms a **barrier** that stops moisture from the filling soaking into the bread, it adds flavour and moistness, and it helps to hold the filling in place.

ul: Spread only needs to be soft, not melted. If it is hard from the fridge and tears the bread, soften it a little first at room temperature, and then spread it thinly.
Use a palette knife or a flat knife, and spread to all four edges.
Other spreads: mustard, cream cheese, avocado (pear) mashed with lime and salt, relishes.

head: Filling
How it is prepared
Care
rows: Egg mayonnaise
Hard-boiled eggs cooled, chopped and mixed with mayonnaise, salt and pepper.
High risk. Allergen: egg. Keep chilled.
Tuna mayonnaise
Drained tinned tuna mixed with mayonnaise and chopped onion or celery.
High risk. Allergens: fish, egg. Drain well, or the filling will be wet.
Chicken salad
Cooked, chilled chicken, diced, with mayonnaise.
High risk. Cool the chicken before mixing.
Ham and cheese
Sliced ham and cheese, with mustard or butter.
Allergens: milk. Keep chilled.
Cucumber and cream cheese
Thinly sliced, dried cucumber with cream cheese.
Allergen: milk. Pat cucumber dry.
Ackee and saltfish
Cooked ackee and saltfish, cooled quickly and chilled.
Allergen: fish. Use the ackee only when it has been prepared safely.
Jerk chicken
Cooked jerk chicken, sliced, with lettuce and mayonnaise.
Cooked to 74 °C, cooled, chilled. Spicy: tell guests.
Avocado (pear)
Mashed with lime juice and salt, or sliced.
Prepare late; it browns.
Callaloo and cheese
Cooked callaloo, well drained and cooled, with cheese.
Drain well to avoid wet bread. Allergen: milk.

ul: A **binder** such as mayonnaise holds a filling of chopped tuna, chicken or egg together.
Put **wet fillings** (tomato, cucumber, a moist spread) between **drier layers** (lettuce, cheese or ham), never directly on the bread, so the bread does not go soggy.
Drain tuna, callaloo and tomato; pat cucumber and lettuce dry.
Weigh or measure the filling for each sandwich so that portions are equal and cost is controlled.

blocks.p: A garnish for a sandwich platter should be edible and suit the food: **parsley, cress, cherry tomatoes, cucumber twists, lettuce leaves, a slice of lime**. Keep it small and fresh.

head: Type
What it is
Example
When served
rows: Closed sandwich
Filling between two slices of bread.
Ham and cheese; egg mayonnaise on hard dough bread
Lunches, picnics, packed meals.
Open sandwich
One slice of bread or toast, with the topping on show.
Smoked marlin and cream cheese; ackee and saltfish
Light lunches and receptions; eaten with a knife and fork.
Club sandwich
Three slices of toast with two layers of filling.
Chicken or turkey, bacon, lettuce, tomato and mayonnaise
Lunch menus and room service.
Finger (tea) sandwich
A small sandwich with the crusts cut off, cut into strips or triangles.
Cucumber and cream cheese; egg mayonnaise
Afternoon tea and receptions.
Pinwheel
A spread and filling rolled up in bread or a wrap, chilled and sliced into rounds.
Cream cheese and ham in a wrap
Parties and buffets.
Wrap
A filling rolled up in a soft flat bread.
Callaloo and cheese; chicken and lettuce
Lunches, picnics, take-away.
Toasted (grilled) sandwich or panini
A filled sandwich heated in a press or grill.
Jerk chicken and cheese panini; grilled cheese
Hot snacks and lunches.
Canapé
A one-bite open sandwich on a small base.
Solomon Gundy on a cracker
Cocktail parties and receptions.

flow: Lay the bread slices out in pairs, in a row
Spread the bread thinly with butter or another spread, right to the edges
Put the filling on one slice of each pair: weighed amount, spread evenly to the edges, with drier layers next to the bread
Cover with the second slice, buttered side down
Press lightly
Cut with a sharp serrated knife into triangles, fingers or squares
Plate, garnish, cover and chill
Toast three slices of bread until golden; let them cool a little so they do not melt the spread
Spread a little mayonnaise or butter on one side of each
On the first slice put lettuce, tomato and sliced chicken or turkey
Put the second slice on top; add bacon, more lettuce and tomato
Cover with the third slice, mayonnaise side down; press lightly
Insert four cocktail sticks, one near each corner; cut into **four triangles** (cut corner to corner both ways), through the sticks
Stand the triangles on a plate with a garnish and a side such as crisps or a small salad

blocks.note: Cocktail sticks are sharp. Count them in and count them out, and warn the guest that the sticks are there.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Use thin-sliced bread. Spread the soft butter or spread right to the edges.
Cut the crusts off with a sharp serrated knife, then cut each sandwich into three fingers or four small triangles.
Fillings must be soft and thinly spread (cucumber slices very thin and patted dry; egg mayonnaise; cream cheese).
Cover with a clean damp (not wet) cloth or cling film so they do not dry out; chill.
Warm the tortilla slightly if it is stiff, so it does not crack.
Spread the wrap right to the edge, put a line of filling along the middle, leaving a gap at the edges, and fold in the sides before you roll tightly.
Cut a wrap in half on the slant for a neat look.

**Pinwheels:** spread with cream cheese or another soft spread, add a thin layer of filling, roll up tightly, wrap in cling film and **chill** so that it is firm, then slice with a sharp knife into rounds.

ol: Check the press or grill: clean, the cable and plug undamaged. Switch on and let it heat as the maker says.
Prepare the sandwich: chilled, cooked filling (such as jerk chicken), cheese, and thin vegetables; butter the **outside** of the bread lightly.
Close the press. Do not overfill, or the filling will push out and burn.
Cook until the bread is golden and the filling is piping hot (reheated filling about 74 °C) and the cheese has melted.
Lift out with **tongs**: the plates are very hot.
Cut and serve at once; hold hot at 63 °C or above if there is a delay.

ul: Never put your fingers between the hot plates, and keep hands dry when you plug in or switch on.

Switch off at the switch and unplug when finished. Clean it only when it is **off, unplugged and cool**: wipe the plates with a damp cloth, and scrape off burnt cheese with a plastic tool, not a metal knife.
Jamaica's supply is 110 V, 50 Hz. Check that equipment is made for it and report a cracked plug or cable.

blocks.p: When you have to make a lot of sandwiches, the quickest way is a **production line** (assembly line). Instead of making each sandwich from start to finish, every person does one stage, and the work moves along the table. A line is faster, and every sandwich comes out the same.

flow: Wash hands; clean and sanitise the benches and boards; put on gloves
Put out only what is needed for the first batch; keep the rest in the fridge
Lay out all the slices of bread in pairs, in rows (the **laying-out** stage)
Person 1: spread the bread right to the edges
Person 2: fill with the weighed amount of filling and add the drier layer
Person 3: close the sandwiches and press them lightly
Person 4: cut, remove crusts if needed, and plate
Cover each tray and chill; label

ul: Use one filling at a time, and keep the other fillings in the fridge.
Do the **special-diet sandwiches first**, with clean equipment, before the filling and crumbs of the main order can spread to them.
Use tongs or clean disposable gloves; change gloves when they tear or when you change tasks.
Keep the work space clear. Do not leave open bread bags or filling bowls out beside the line.
Use a **scoop or spoon of the same size**, or weigh, so that the filling is even and goes to the edges.
Check the first sandwich of each batch; correct the filling, the spread and the cut; then carry on.
Use a **sharp serrated bread knife** and a gentle sawing action, with little downward pressure. A blunt knife squashes the sandwich and tears the bread.
Cut on a clean, steady board, and wipe the knife between cuts if the filling is sticky.
A square sandwich cut corner to corner gives **2 triangles**; cut corner to corner both ways, it gives **4 triangles**. Cut straight across twice for 4 squares, or into 3 fingers.
Cutters give shapes such as rounds, hearts and stars for children or special parties. Use the offcuts for breadcrumbs, not for the guests.
Check each sandwich: neat, evenly filled, cleanly cut, with filling to the edges.

head: Fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Soggy bread
No spread barrier; wet filling next to bread; made too early; wet leaves.
Spread butter to the edges; use drier layers next to the bread; dry salad; assemble late.
Torn bread
Spread too hard and cold; knife too blunt.
Soften the spread slightly; use a flat knife and a light touch.
Squashed, ragged cuts
Blunt knife; too much pressure.
Use a sharp serrated knife with a gentle sawing action.
Uneven fillings
Fillings not weighed or spread; no check.
Weigh or use a standard scoop; spread to the edges.
Dry, curled bread
Left uncovered.
Cover with cling film or a lid at once.
Filling falls out
Filling too wet or too thick; overfilled.
Drain well; use the right amount; use a binder.

blocks.p: Many guests cannot eat everything on the menu. Ask early, write it on the order, and tell the head cook.

head: Guest
What to avoid
Hidden sources in sandwiches
rows: Coeliac disease or gluten-free diet
Wheat, barley, rye and oats (gluten); even small crumbs can harm.
Ordinary bread, wraps, crackers, some sauces and processed meats; crumbs on boards, knives and in the butter.
Egg allergy
Egg in any form.
Egg mayonnaise, mayonnaise, some breads and glazes.
Milk allergy
Milk, butter, cheese, cream cheese, yoghurt.
Butter spread; cheese; some breads and margarines contain milk.
Fish or shellfish allergy
Fish, shrimp, crab, lobster.
Tuna, Solomon Gundy, shrimp, fish sauces.
Sesame, nut or soya allergy
The named food.
Buns with sesame seeds, nut spreads, some margarines and breads.
Vegetarian
Meat, poultry, fish.
Ham, chicken, tuna; check mayonnaise and cheese labels.
Vegan
All animal products including egg, milk and honey.
Butter, mayonnaise, cheese; use vegan spread and plant-based fillings such as avocado or hummus.

flow: Wash hands and put on clean gloves
Clean and sanitise the board, knife and bench; use a clean knife and a **fresh, separate tub of spread** (not one that has had crumbs of ordinary bread in it)
Make the gluten-free sandwiches **first**, before any ordinary bread comes out
Check every filling label for gluten
Cut with the clean knife
Cover, label clearly ('Gluten-free') and keep them apart from the others
Serve them to the guest directly, or on their own labelled plate

ul: A **crumb** of ordinary bread can be enough to make a coeliac guest ill. Cross-contact is the problem, not only the ingredients.
Do not toast gluten-free bread in a toaster or press used for ordinary bread, unless the equipment is clean or has a clean bag or liner.
Mayonnaise contains egg, so a guest with an egg allergy needs an egg-free spread such as oil and lime or avocado.

blocks.note: Treat every allergy as serious, even if the guest says it is 'only mild'. Never guess: if you are not sure of an ingredient, check the label or ask the head cook. Label the allergens on every tray and on the buffet.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Choose a clean platter of the right size, lined with a doily or a bed of lettuce.
Cut the sandwiches into **even shapes** (triangles, fingers or squares) with clean edges.
Arrange them in **neat rows** or a pattern, grouped by filling, with the **cut side and fillings facing out** so guests can see what is inside.
Do not overfill the platter. Leave a little space.
Garnish with parsley, cress or cherry tomatoes, put at one end or in the centre.
Label the platter or each row with the fillings and any allergens.
For a buffet, keep spare platters in the fridge and bring them out one at a time.

blocks.p: Serve on a clean, whole plate with a side of salad or crisps and a garnish. Wipe the rim. A club sandwich stands on its cut side with sticks showing. An open sandwich is arranged so that the topping is visible and neat.

ul: Neat, evenly filled, cleanly cut, with no gaps in the filling or dry edges.
Right temperature: cold sandwiches cold, hot sandwiches hot.
Correct label and allergens.
Clean platter and rim; garnish fresh.

flow: Cover, label and chill the sandwiches
Throw away any filling that has been out too long
Scrape and wash boards, knives and bowls in hot soapy water
Rinse, then sanitise with a food-safe sanitiser; air-dry
Switch off, unplug, cool and clean the sandwich press
Wipe the benches; empty bins; mop with a wet-floor sign
Wash your hands; report faults and low stock

blocks.note: Never mix bleach with other cleaning products, because the mix can give off a poisonous gas. Follow the label and the Centre's rules.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A serrated bread knife has a long blade with a saw-like edge. Carry it point down, close to your side.
Cut on a steady board, with the fingers of your guiding hand curled back.
Never try to catch a falling knife. Wash knives one at a time.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I make the gluten-free sandwiches first with clean equipment, so that crumbs from ordinary bread cannot get onto them.'
blocks.label: Tip

A sandwich of three slices of toast, usually cut into four triangles.
A small, crustless sandwich cut into strips.
A rolled sandwich, chilled and sliced into rounds.
A filling rolled in a soft flat bread.
A sandwich toasted in a ridged press, in a crusty roll.
A small one-bite open sandwich on a base.
A flat bread that opens up into a pocket.
A dense Jamaican white loaf, often used for sandwiches.
A soft Jamaican folded bread, often used for patties.
Hard and dry, as bread that has been left uncovered.
Butter, margarine or mayonnaise put on bread to keep it from going soggy.
An ingredient such as mayonnaise that holds a filling together.
Food in which bacteria grow easily and which is eaten without more cooking.
About 5 °C to 63 °C, where bacteria grow fastest.
Making many sandwiches in stages, each person doing one stage.
The written recipe a kitchen always uses, so a dish is the same every time.
A substance in food that can cause a harmful reaction in some people.
An illness in which gluten damages the gut, so the person must avoid gluten.
Allergen traces passing from one food to another, for example through crumbs or a shared knife.
First in, first out: use the older stock first.
A lacy paper placed under sandwiches on a platter.
A small edible decoration on a dish.

c1.title: Packed lunches for a Blue Mountains hike
c1.text: A villa in Irish Town has 12 guests going on an all-day walk in the Blue Mountains, leaving at 7:00 a.m. They will eat lunch at about 12:30 p.m., five and a half hours later, and it will be hot. The cook, Sandra, plans egg mayonnaise and ham and cheese sandwiches. She has one cool box and a freezer with ice packs.

c2.title: Sixty sandwiches for a wedding brunch in Ocho Rios
c2.text: A hotel in Ocho Rios has ordered 60 closed sandwiches for a wedding brunch at 11:00 a.m. Chef Anthony plans one sandwich as two slices of bread, about 10 g of butter and 50 g of filling. A sliced loaf gives 20 usable slices. The ingredients for the whole order cost JMD 9,000. The chicken for the filling has just come out of the oven at 7:30 a.m.

c3.title: Afternoon tea with special diets in Mandeville
c3.text: A guest house in Mandeville is serving afternoon tea for ten, including one guest with coeliac disease, one child allergic to egg and one vegetarian. The cook, Michelle, plans cucumber and cream cheese, egg mayonnaise and ham sandwiches. The same tub of butter is on the bench, and has crumbs of ordinary bread in it.

c4.title: Hot sandwiches for a pool party in Negril
c4.text: At a villa in Negril, trainee Jermaine is making jerk chicken and cheese paninis in the sandwich press for a pool party. The jerk chicken was cooked yesterday and kept in the fridge. He notices that the cable on the press has a cut in its covering. He overfills the sandwiches, and cheese oozes out onto the plates.

c5.title: A tray of poor sandwiches in Treasure Beach
c5.text: Trainee Rochelle has made a tray of ham, tomato and cheese sandwiches at a guest house in Treasure Beach. The bread is soggy, torn in places and the cuts are squashed and ragged. She had put cold, hard butter straight from the fridge on the bread, sliced the tomato wet directly on the bread and cut them with a short, blunt paring knife, a long time before service.

c6.title: Eighty sandwiches in a hurry in Montego Bay
c6.text: At a hotel in Montego Bay, trainee Ricardo is making 80 tuna mayonnaise sandwiches. He puts the whole bowl of tuna filling on the bench. After an hour and a half, the bowl is nearly empty, and he tips fresh filling from the fridge into the same bowl.

questions.q: How should Sandra pack the sandwiches for the hike?
o: Cold, wrapped and in the cool box with ice packs
Made the evening before and packed in a bag at room temperature
Frozen solid and then packed in a bag left out in the sun
Packed while still warm, so that they stay soft until lunch
questions.why: High-risk sandwiches must stay at 5 °C or below. A cool box with ice packs, packed just before leaving, keeps them cold. Bags at room temperature or a hot bag keep food in the danger zone.

questions.q: Which filling is the lower-risk choice for such a long, hot trip?
o: Egg mayonnaise with chopped onion
Tuna mayonnaise with chopped celery
Cheese and cucumber
Chicken salad with mayonnaise
questions.why: Fillings with mayonnaise, egg, fish or cooked meat grow bacteria easily when they warm. Cheese with a fresh vegetable is lower-risk, though it still needs to be kept cool.

questions.q: What should the guests be told about leftover sandwiches?
o: Eat them for supper, because they were made fresh that morning
Throw them away after the plan's time, and not take them home
Put them in a bag in the sun, so that any germs are killed
Keep them in a bag for tomorrow's breakfast at the villa
questions.why: Sandwiches that have been warm for hours may hold dangerous levels of bacteria, even if they look and smell fine. After the safe time, they are thrown away.

questions.q: How many loaves does Anthony need for 60 sandwiches (before extra for waste)?
o: 3 loaves
7 loaves
6 loaves
12 loaves
questions.why: 60 sandwiches need 120 slices. A loaf gives 20 usable slices, so 120 ÷ 20 = 6 loaves. He should order a spare loaf for waste.

questions.q: How much filling does he need for the whole order?
o: 30 kg
3 kg
1.2 kg
questions.why: 50 g × 60 sandwiches = 3,000 g, which is 3 kg. Check that you have changed grams to kilograms correctly: 1,000 g = 1 kg.

questions.q: What is the cost of one sandwich?
o: JMD 15
JMD 150
JMD 540
questions.why: Cost per sandwich = total cost ÷ number of sandwiches = 9,000 ÷ 60 = JMD 150. Weighing the filling keeps this cost the same for every sandwich.

questions.q: What should Anthony do with the chicken before it goes into the filling?
o: Mix it in at once, while it is hot, for the best flavour
Leave it on the bench until it is just warm to the touch
Wash it under the cold tap to cool it down quickly
Cool it quickly and chill it before mixing it in
questions.why: Hot chicken warms the mayonnaise and the other fillings and lets bacteria grow in a high-risk filling. Spread the chicken on a tray or in shallow containers to cool quickly, then chill.

questions.q: In what order should Michelle make the sandwiches?
o: The ordinary sandwiches first, then the special-diet ones
All of them together, using the same board and knife
Special-diet ones first, on clean equipment
The egg sandwiches first, so that they have time to chill
questions.why: Making allergy and special-diet sandwiches first, with clean equipment, keeps crumbs and traces of egg or gluten from the ordinary ones from reaching them.

questions.q: What should she do about the butter with crumbs in it?
o: Scrape the crumbs off the top and then use the butter
Use it as it is, because butter has no gluten in it
Melt the butter, so that the crumbs sink to the bottom
Use a fresh, separate tub for gluten-free ones
questions.why: Crumbs of ordinary bread carry gluten, and a small amount can make a coeliac guest ill. The butter is contaminated and must not be used for that guest.

questions.q: Which filling and spread suit the child with an egg allergy?
o: Ham with butter, with labels checked for egg
Egg mayonnaise on thin white or brown bread
Cucumber slices with a spread of mayonnaise on top
Ham with a thin layer of mayonnaise on the bread
questions.why: Mayonnaise is made with egg, so any sandwich with mayonnaise or egg filling is unsafe for the child. Ham and butter are suitable if the labels show no egg.

questions.q: What should Jermaine do about the cut in the press cable?
o: Wrap tape round the cut and then use it carefully
Use it with dry hands, since it is only a small cut
Unplug it, mark it 'out of order' and report it
Use it on a wooden table so that it cannot shock him
questions.why: A damaged cable can give an electric shock or cause a fire. The press is taken out of use, unplugged, marked and reported to the supervisor to be repaired.

questions.q: The jerk chicken was cooked yesterday and chilled. How should it be handled in the paninis?
o: Heat the sandwich until the chicken is piping hot
Heat the sandwich until the bread is just golden brown
Heat the sandwich until the cheese has only just softened
Serve it cold from the fridge between slices of toast
questions.why: Reheated food must be piping hot all the way through, about 74 °C, to kill bacteria. Golden bread or soft cheese does not prove the inside is hot enough.

questions.q: How should Jermaine clean the press when the party is over?
o: Switch off, unplug, let it cool, then wipe the plates
Wipe it straight away while it is hot, so the cheese lifts
Pour water over the hot plates to loosen the cheese
Scrape the plates with a metal knife while it is plugged in
questions.why: Never clean electrical equipment while it is plugged in or hot. Switch off, unplug and cool it, then wipe it; use a plastic scraper, not a metal knife, to remove burnt cheese.

questions.q: Why is Rochelle's bread soggy?
o: The bread was far too fresh and soft to hold up the ham
The ham was sliced so thin that it soaked up the butter
The tray was covered with film, so no air reached them
Wet tomato went straight on the bread, hours before service
questions.why: Wet fillings next to the bread, with no barrier, soak into it, especially when the sandwich stands for hours. Put wet fillings between drier layers, spread to the edges, and assemble close to service.

questions.q: Why did the bread tear when she spread the butter?
o: The butter was too soft, and it dragged the bread along
The butter was cold and hard, and needed softening a little
The bread was too stale, and it should have been thrown away
She spread the butter too thinly across each of the slices
questions.why: Hard butter straight from the fridge drags and tears soft bread. Let it soften slightly (not melt) so that it spreads thinly and evenly right to the edges.

questions.q: What would give her cleaner cuts?
o: A short paring knife pressed down hard in a single move
A blunt table knife used with a firm, straight push
A cook's knife wetted with water before each cut
A sharp serrated knife with a gentle sawing action
questions.why: A sharp serrated knife with gentle sawing cuts the crust without squashing the crumb. A short or blunt knife needs force, which squashes the sandwich and tears the bread.

questions.q: What should Ricardo have done with the bowl of tuna filling?
o: Left the whole bowl on the bench, under a clean cloth
Taken out small amounts and kept the rest in the fridge
Put the bowl in the sun, so that the filling stays soft
Stirred the filling now and then, to keep it cool
questions.why: Tuna mayonnaise is high-risk. Take out a small amount at a time and keep the rest at 5 °C or below, so the filling is never in the danger zone for long.

questions.q: What is wrong with tipping fresh filling into the same bowl?
o: The bowl is too small to hold all of the extra filling
Fresh filling is mixed with old filling kept warm too long
The fresh filling will taste different from the old filling
The fresh filling will go soggy when it meets the old filling
questions.why: Bacteria that have grown in the old filling spread into the fresh filling. Throw away old filling that has been out too long, and use a fresh, clean bowl for each batch.

questions.q: A standard recipe uses 40 g of filling for each sandwich. How much filling is needed for 25 sandwiches?
o: 1 kg
10 kg
1.6 kg
questions.why: 40 g × 25 = 1,000 g, which is 1 kg. Weighing filling gives equal portions and keeps the cost the same.

questions.q: Why are pinwheel sandwiches chilled before they are sliced?
o: The filling soaks right into the bread and holds it
The bread dries out and goes crisp, so it is easier to cut
The rolls can be sliced thicker, so there are fewer
The roll goes firm and slices cleanly without breaking up
questions.why: Chilling firms the spread and filling, so the roll holds its shape and a sharp knife cuts neat rounds. A warm, soft roll squashes and the filling squeezes out.
